description: We are a team of three from Brazil, bringing together UX/UI design, front-end, and full-stack development. For this Space Apps Challenge, we took on the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge because fire touches every region we care about, and understanding its patterns can help people prepare before the critical season arrives. Our goal is to turn complex satellite data into something anyone can read, from emergency responders to scientists. Follow our journey! 🌍🔥
summary:
We developed HERU, a web platform that turns more than twenty years of satellite-detected hotspots into a burning activity calendar for any country in the world. Our research object is a problem that distorts the historical record: in 2012, the more detailed VIIRS sensor joined MODIS, and the hotspot count jumped just because the instrument changed. In the United States, it nearly quadrupled from one year to the next.

HERU directly addresses the challenge by harmonizing both sensors onto a single scale, from 2003 to today, for 201 countries and the whole world, with FIRMS data updated every hour. But it goes further: it automatically finds each country's peak season, record year and the months that broke the pattern, and shows the evidence behind every number. Its importance lies in giving fire response planners, scientists and the public a reliable series to understand how burning activity on our planet is changing.
details: HERU: is this month of burning normal? Satellites have been recording hotspots for more than twenty years. That record should show how fire is changing on our planet, but it hides a trap. In 2012, a new satellite with smaller pixels started seeing many more hotspots. The chart shot up, and anyone looking at the number alone would think the world suddenly started burning. The planet didn't change. The satellite did. HERU was built to tell one from the other. What is HERU? HERU is a hotspot calendar for 201 countries and the whole world, from 2003 to today. Each row is a year, each column is a month, and the color shows how many hotspots the satellites recorded. Everything sits on one scale, the VIIRS scale, so 2005 and 2025 can truly be compared. One scale for more than twenty years We used the years when MODIS and VIIRS observed the Earth together (2012 to 2019) to measure how one relates to the other, separately for each 5° block of the planet and for daytime and nighttime overpasses. With that factor, every older MODIS hotspot becomes "VIIRS-equivalent hotspots". We tested the result on years left out of the calibration, and the Methodology page shows the method, the validation and a confidence badge for each country. Each place's pattern, found automatically Pick a country and HERU shows its peak season (the months that hold most of a typical year's hotspots), its record year and the months that broke the pattern. The Anomalies page compares any month, or any chosen period, with what is typical for the same time of year. From the map to the detail A map shows the hotspots of each day for short periods and a monthly grid for longer ones, with the sensor of your choice. Every point explains itself: satellite, time, pixel size and confidence. You can compare two periods side by side, with both maps moving together, or up to four countries, as totals or per 1,000 km² of land. Every number with its proof Every report has a "See evidence" button with the chart behind the number and the data to download as CSV. Nothing on the panel is estimated from the map: the totals come from the daily series, counted hotspot by hotspot. Always up to date Our pipeline downloads FIRMS data since 2000 (665 million hotspots) and publishes a new batch every hour. The website notices new data on its own. Tools we used Pipeline: Python, with pandas, NumPy, PyArrow (Parquet files), Shapely (the country of each hotspot) and Requests, running on a Linux server. Website: TypeScript, React and Next.js, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL for the map and the globe, Three.js for the globe and the 3D calendar, and Motion for animations. Data: FIRMS (MODIS, VIIRS and Landsat), with near real-time data from LANCE. Server: nginx, serving the website and the data on the same domain. Open source code: https://github.com/orgs/HERU-Project-Nasa/repositories Our mission We want the history of burning to be read by what happened on the ground, not by a satellite swap. When the line goes up in HERU, the planet changed. And understanding that is the first step to following how fire responds to the climate crisis.
